models.collectorNote: Air-cooled cars (pre-1998) live in their own market. Documentation and original specification decide values more than mileage does.

generations.name: 964 — the bridge car
generations.note: The bridge car: classic silhouette over modern underpinnings, with all-wheel drive available for the first time. The Turbo and Carrera RS are the blue chips.

generations.name: 993 — last of the air-cooled
generations.note: The last air-cooled 911, and the market treats it accordingly. Multi-link rear suspension finally tamed the layout's worst habits.

generations.name: 992 — the modern benchmark
generations.note: Wide-body for everyone, a proper digital cabin, and a Turbo S that out-accelerates most hypercars. The GT3 keeps a 9,000 rpm naturally aspirated flat-six alive.

models.intro: One car, perfected for sixty years. The engine is still in the wrong place, the silhouette is still a teardrop, and the 911 is still the sports car everything else is judged against — because Porsche never stopped developing it.

generations.name: First generation
generations.note: Launched with V8s only, including a 450 hp Turbo when that was absurd for an SUV. Low-range gearing meant it could actually climb things.

generations.name: Second generation
generations.note: Lighter, better looking, and hybridised. The diesel suited it so well that its loss stung.

generations.name: Third generation
generations.note: Turbo V6s and V8s, a Coupe variant chasing the X6, and a Turbo GT that laps the Nürburgring faster than sports cars.

models.intro: The SUV that saved Porsche — purists hated it in 2002 and the profits funded every GT car since. It also happened to be genuinely good: fast, capable off-road, and unmistakably a Porsche to drive.
models.name: Cayenne

generations.name: First generation
generations.note: Launched as Turbo and Turbo S — no turbo anywhere, the names are trim levels now. The 2024 facelift brought more range, more power, and the 1,000 hp-class Turbo GT.

models.intro: Porsche's first EV, built to answer one question: can an electric car feel like a Porsche? Two-speed rear gearbox, repeatable launch control, and steering that talks. The answer held up.
models.name: Taycan

models.collectorNote: Speedsters and four-cam Carreras are the seven-figure end of the market. Matching numbers and the Kardex build record are everything on any 356.

generations.name: 356 (original)
generations.note: Hand-built early cars, split windscreens at first, and engines that grew from 1.1 to 1.5 litres as Porsche found its feet.

generations.name: 356C
generations.note: Disc brakes all round and the most developed pushrod flat-four. The SC was the quick one; the 911 was already waiting in the wings.

models.intro: The first production Porsche: a Beetle-derived aluminium coupe built in a sawmill in Gmünd, Austria, that became the template for everything after. Light, slippery, and quicker than cars with twice the power.

models.collectorNote: The 981 GT4 and 718 GT4 RS / Spyder RS are the collectible end. Six-cylinder cars generally hold value far better than the turbo fours.

generations.name: Boxster (first generation)
generations.note: The roadster that paid for the 911's future. Mid-engined balance and a flat-six soundtrack for relatively sensible money.

generations.name: Cayman/Boxster (third generation)
generations.note: The six-cylinder peak before downsizing. The Cayman GT4 got the 911's 3.8 and a manual only — an instant classic.

generations.name: 718 (fourth generation)
generations.note: Turbo fours for the standard cars drew the complaints; the GTS 4.0, GT4 RS and Spyder RS answered them with a 9,000 rpm six taken from the GT3.

models.intro: The Boxster saved Porsche in the 1990s; the Cayman coupe followed in 2005, and the pair became the handling benchmark money could buy. Renamed 718 in 2016 for the turbo flat-four era, then redeemed by the 4.0-litre sixes. Production of the petrol cars ended in 2025, with an electric successor planned.
models.name: 718 Cayman/Boxster
